Electronic music radio promotion for independent artists

By the RadioReach team Updated August 18, 2026 2 min read Genre playbooks

On this page
  • Pitch shows, not stations
  • The electronic radio map
  • Radio edits, extended mixes, and versions
  • DJ mixes, sessions, and guest slots
  • What electronic show hosts ask for

Electronic music barely exists on radio as "stations" — it exists as shows. Two-hour techno programs at midnight, ambient Sunday mornings, bass-music Fridays, community slots hosted by DJs who also run labels and club nights. For an independent producer, that is good news: the decision-maker is usually one reachable human with a taste for novelty, not a committee. This guide covers how dance and electronic artists actually get played.

Pitch shows, not stations

A single community station might carry a breakfast pop show, a jazz program, and a warehouse-techno mix — same transmitter, different planets. Research at the show level: find the programs whose recent tracklists sit next to yours, and pitch the host by name. A perfect show match at a 200-watt station beats a generic drop to a station that barely programs dance music.

The electronic radio map

  • Community radio: the beating heart of dance programming — eclectic stations with dedicated electronic and ambient shows, often streaming globally.
  • Internet radio platforms: station collectives and independent broadcasters where entire schedules are DJ-curated. Highest acceptance rate for unreleased and independent material.
  • College radio: electronic directors and EDM/electronic chart reporting; strong for crossover-leaning records.
  • Specialty mixes on larger stations: late-night dance slots, usually locked to established DJs — a target for later, once you have a story.

Radio edits, extended mixes, and versions

Dance music has a versioning culture radio expects you to speak fluently:

  • Radio edit: tightened arrangement, clean arrangement intro/outro — your default for general programming
  • Extended / club mix: for show hosts and mix DJs
  • Remixes: alternate angles for the same show, or a way onto shows that skipped the original
  • Clean edit: required for anything broadcast-safe if there are vocals

Label them clearly in one link. Hosts remember the artists who made their prep easy.

DJ mixes, sessions, and guest slots

Electronic shows often want more than a track: a guest mix, a short interview, or a premiere. Offering a 30-minute guest mix — easy to produce if you already DJ — is one of the highest-conversion asks in the genre, because it gives the host a full episode of programming, not three minutes of it.

What electronic show hosts ask for

  • A streaming link that doesn't expire the week after your release
  • WAVs available on request, not attached to the first email
  • BPM and key, listed — hosts blend tracks live
  • A one-line genre self-description that doesn't require decoding
  • Proof other shows played you, once you have it

That's a modest list, and most pitches fail half of it. Nailing it puts you in the top tier of submissions any host receives — the EPK guide shows how to keep it all in one link.

Frequently asked questions

Should I pitch the club mix or a radio edit to stations?

Both, clearly labeled. A show host building a Friday-night mix wants the extended version; a daytime music director wants a tight edit. Hosting both in your EPK link with honest labels (radio edit 3:42 / extended 6:18) makes you easy to program either way.

Is internet radio worth pitching for electronic music?

Yes — some of the most influential electronic programming in the world is online, show-hosted, and open to direct submissions. A spin on a respected internet show carries real credibility with listeners, clubs, and labels, even without an FM dial position.

Do remixes help get radio play?

A well-chosen remix gives a host two reasons to feature you — the original plus a fresh take — and can out-perform the source track in club-oriented shows. Pitch the strongest version first and mention the other exists.
